case_study_insert.main_stem: Castlewick Chain Drives (CCD) is a public limited company in the industrial power-transmission sector near Wolverhampton, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 1998 by Marcus Castlewick, it manufactures chain, sprocket and coupling drives for factory conveyor systems throughout the region and uses a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. CCD plans to invest $1,200,000 in an automated heat-treatment line, financed by a $700,000 share issue and a $500,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. CCD faces rising absenteeism, now 8%, and growing metal waste in its heat-treatment process.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Log — Q4 2025: The Wolverhampton plant heat-treated 28,400 chain and sprocket units last quarter, with a recorded metal-waste rate of 6.4%, down from 8.1% a year earlier. Absenteeism reached 8% of shifts. Delivery lead time averaged 9 days against a 6-day target. A survey of 350 factory procurement managers found that 61% rank reliable delivery above price and 39% would pay up to $0.80 more for certified heat-treated drives. A training audit shows 26 of 120 staff need coupling-assembly retraining; in-house coaching is offered, while external courses cost $620 per employee.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, raising borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $13.10 to $13.91 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills across engineering. (3) Steel alloy and energy input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, while factory conveyor investment grew 3.1%.

questions.question_text: CCD plans to fund part of its $1,200,000 heat-treatment line with a $500,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for CCD of financing it through the $700,000 share issue instead.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue raises $700,000 with no interest charge and no fixed repayment dates, so CCD avoids adding debt service on top of fixed costs of $480,000 a year. That protects cash flow while the automated heat-treatment line is commissioned and helps absorb the 6.2% minimum wage rise and the 11.3% rise in alloy and energy inputs without raising the $20.00 selling price. Retained earnings are not committed to lenders, so more cash stays inside the business.

Point 2: Equity does not have to be secured against the Wolverhampton plant, so the $2,950,000 of non-current assets are not exposed to repossession if factory conveyor demand weakens. For a public limited company, a share issue also broadens the shareholder base and supports a larger capital structure for future expansion, whereas the $500,000 bank loan would add fixed interest and repayment pressure on a business already employing 120 staff with 8% absenteeism. The $700,000 can therefore fund the $1,200,000 line without competing with the $480,000 fixed costs for cash.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to CCD and its $1,200,000 financing decision.

questions.question_text: CCD is launching its certified heat-treated drive range. Consider national trade-press advertising, sponsorship of a factory-automation exhibition, or a direct sales team calling on conveyor manufacturers. Which should CCD choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National trade-press advertising: Placing adverts in engineering journals would reach procurement managers across factory conveyor firms and support the claim of certified heat treatment. However, print campaigns are expensive, hard to measure and largely untargeted, so a firm already committing $1,200,000 to a new line and $480,000 a year in fixed costs would waste much of the spend on readers who do not buy drives.

Factory-automation exhibition sponsorship: An exhibition stand lets engineers inspect the heat-treated chains and sprockets and question CCD's team about the 6.4% waste rate and quality controls. It matches the 61% of surveyed managers who rank reliable delivery above price, since face-to-face discussion can reassure them. The disadvantages are the cost of the stand and the short window for follow-up, so leads must be converted quickly.

Direct sales team: A dedicated team calling on conveyor manufacturers could build long-term relationships and explain the $0.80 premium for certified drives to the 39% of buyers who would pay more. It gives full control of the message and fast feedback, but recruiting and funding a team for a 120-employee firm with 8% absenteeism adds significant fixed cost and takes time to produce results.

Recommendation: CCD should choose the factory-automation exhibition sponsorship as the main launch route, backed by light follow-up from existing sales staff. Technical buyers value inspecting drives, and the exhibition reaches certifiers of the 61% who prioritise delivery. Trade press is rejected as unmeasurable and broad; a new direct sales team is rejected because its added fixed cost and slow payback would strain the $500,000 bank loan and $480,000 fixed costs, though selected calls should follow up exhibition leads.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to CCD.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in the context of CCD with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of CCD with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade press and a new sales team are rejected.

questions.question_text: CCD's absenteeism has reached 8% and metal waste is rising. Explain two benefits for CCD of changing from autocratic leadership to a more democratic style in its heat-treatment plant.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership would let the 120 employees, especially heat-treatment operators, suggest practical ways to cut the 6.4% metal-waste rate. Operators know the furnace settings best, so their ideas can reduce waste without further capital spending on the $1,200,000 line. In Maslow's terms, being consulted satisfies esteem needs, which should lift morale and help reduce the 8% absenteeism that disrupts the hierarchical structure and delays the 9-day delivery target.

Point 2: Involvement builds commitment and trust, lowering labour turnover and the need to retrain the 26 staff identified in the skills audit at $620 per employee. Herzberg would see added responsibility as a motivator, so staff take more care over coupling assembly. In a large public limited company, listening to operators also improves communication upward through the hierarchy, so problems with the automated heat-treatment line are reported early, protecting output of 120,000 drives and the eight-dollar contribution on each $20.00 unit.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CCD's absenteeism, waste, workforce and retraining costs.

questions.question_text: CCD must retrain 26 staff for the new heat-treatment line. Consider in-house coaching or external courses at $620 per employee. Which should CCD choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
In-house coaching: Training on the Wolverhampton line is specific to CCD's furnaces and coupling-assembly standards and avoids the $620 per person fee for 26 staff, a saving of $16,120 (26 × $620). Coaching keeps operators productive and lets them tackle the 6.4% metal-waste rate immediately, which matters with 8% absenteeism already reducing shifts. The weaknesses are that coaches are production staff whose own output suffers, bad habits may spread, and there is no external certificate, which could matter for a public limited company supplying certified heat-treated drives.

External courses: At $620 each the 26 staff would cost $16,120, small next to the $1,200,000 investment and easier to schedule away from the plant. Outside providers bring current heat-treatment theory and a recognised qualification, valuable with 8% absenteeism and support for the 61% of buyers who rank reliable delivery first. However, staff are away from the plant, reducing capacity on the new line, and generic content may not match CCD's exact heat-treatment settings, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: CCD should choose in-house coaching first, with short external modules for supervisors. Coaching is machine-specific, cheaper and avoids output loss while waste is 6.4% and absence 8%. Full external training is rejected because sending 26 staff off-site and spending $16,120 would slow commissioning of the $1,200,000 line and still require on-site reinforcement; certification can be added later once the process is stable and the 9-day delivery target is secure. This also protects the 9-day delivery target, the effort to cut 6.4% waste and the cover of $480,000 fixed costs.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to CCD.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of CCD.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in the context of CCD with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CCD's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $480,000 ÷ ($20.00 − $12.00) = $480,000 ÷ $8.00 = 60,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 60,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $20.00 − $12.00 = $8.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $8.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CCD's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 60,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 120,000 drives gives a margin of safety of 60,000 units, showing a large cushion before the $1,200,000 heat-treatment line fails to cover its costs.
2. Contribution of $8.00 a drive lets managers test pricing, for example the $0.80 premium for certified drives would lift contribution to $8.80, helping recover the $480,000 fixed costs sooner.
3. Fixed costs of $480,000 and $8.00 contribution indicate the sales volume needed to service the $500,000 bank loan, so targets can be set for conveyor manufacturers before further borrowing.
4. Average total cost of $16.00 a drive ($480,000 ÷ 120,000 = $4.00 plus $12.00) can be tracked against the 6.4% metal-waste rate to judge whether the automated line is reducing waste and improving unit cost quarter by quarter.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 60,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $8.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 120,000-unit output; certified-drive premium modelling; loan-service volume for the $500,000 borrowing; and average total cost of $16.00 to monitor waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CCD's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has CCD's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.83 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.73 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.13 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.14 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 inventories + $260,000 trade receivables + $80,000 cash = $550,000; 2025 current assets = $190,000 + $310,000 + $55,000 = $555,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives 2024 = $550,000 ÷ $300,000 = 1.83 and 2025 = $555,000 ÷ $320,000 = 1.73. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($550,000 − $210,000) ÷ $300,000 = $340,000 ÷ $300,000 = 1.13; 2025 = ($555,000 − $190,000) ÷ $320,000 = $365,000 ÷ $320,000 = 1.14.

Evaluation: Liquidity has not improved overall. The current ratio fell from 1.83 to 1.73 because current liabilities rose from $300,000 to $320,000 while current assets barely moved from $550,000 to $555,000. The acid test was almost flat, rising from 1.13 to 1.14, so the underlying position is little better even after excluding inventories. The concerning movement is trade receivables climbing from $260,000 to $310,000 while cash fell from $80,000 to $55,000, suggesting sales are being made but cash is not being collected. With a $500,000 bank loan to service and $480,000 fixed costs a year, that cash drain matters more than the small current-asset increase.

Conclusion: CCD's financial position has not improved. The current ratio worsened from 1.83 to 1.73 and the acid test only edged from 1.13 to 1.14, so liquidity is slightly weaker, not stronger. The sharp rise in receivables and fall in cash are the main causes; management should tighten credit control before relying on the $700,000 share issue to fund further expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables, cash and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CCD of introducing statistical quality control to reduce its 6.4% metal-waste rate.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Statistical quality control would identify variation in the heat-treatment process so CCD can cut the 6.4% metal-waste rate toward the 8.1% improvement already seen. Less waste lowers the $12.00 variable cost per unit, protecting the $8.00 contribution on each $20.00 drive and supporting the 61% of surveyed managers who rank reliable delivery above price. Fewer faulty drives also help the 39% who would pay $0.80 more for certified heat-treated drives, since consistent quality makes that premium credible.

Disadvantage: Installing inspection systems and training 120 staff to use them adds cost at a time when fixed costs are $480,000 a year and a $500,000 bank loan is being serviced. With 8% absenteeism, data collection may be inconsistent, and quality control detects problems rather than preventing them, so waste may fall only slowly unless the automated $1,200,000 line itself is recalibrated. The 9-day lead time could also lengthen while staff learn the new procedures, weakening the 61% delivery-focused segment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CCD's waste rate, research data and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in steel alloy and energy input costs will affect CCD. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If CCD's $500,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by the 0.75 percentage-point rise × $500,000 = $3,750 a year (0.0075 × $500,000). That is small against fixed costs of $480,000 and can be eliminated if the loan is fixed-rate. The $700,000 share issue is not affected by interest rates, though a higher rate may depress the share price if CCD ever needs further equity.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $13.91 an hour): The insert gives a workforce of 120 but not hours worked, individual pay or how many are on the minimum, so an annual wage total cannot be invented honestly. What can be derived is labour productivity: 120,000 drives ÷ 120 staff = 1,000 drives per worker. With 8% absenteeism, lost shifts reduce that figure and raise unit labour cost, squeezing the $8.00 contribution. The effect is significant but cannot be precisely quantified from the data provided.

Input cost inflation (11.3% on alloy and energy): The insert does not split the $12.00 variable cost, so only an explicitly labelled upper bound is defensible: if the whole $12.00 rose 11.3%, that adds 11.3% × $12.00 = $1.36 per drive, and at 120,000 drives a year that is $162,000 (120,000 × $1.36). A partial rise would still compound across all output and directly cut contribution, though the $0.80 certified premium from the survey could recover part.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in alloy and energy inputs will have the greatest impact. Its $162,000 upper bound dwarfs the $3,750 interest effect, it applies to every one of the 120,000 drives, and it erodes the $8.00 contribution that must cover $480,000 fixed costs. The interest rise is small and hedgeable by fixing the rate; the wage rise matters through absenteeism but cannot be quantified from the insert and can be partly offset by productivity of 1,000 drives per worker.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to CCD.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CCD with shown calculations where data allow.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of CCD using only shown derivations from insert figures and a well-justified greatest-impact judgment.
